\pard\cf1\f0\fs22 Ashley Bernal-Assistant Town Manager-introduced Dr. Samantha Danchuk and Brooks Barton (project engineer) with APTIM.\par

Dr. Danchuk-provided project overview; work completed in area of survey, wells, sampling, design, evaluation; presented physical survey results, loss of 3.5 feet in less than 2 years; erosion occurring impacting natural habitat in area; concept design alternatives to have low impact.\par
\par
Mr. Barton discussed alternative 1A which uses a single layer revetment, provided an example; 1B is a double layer revetment, discussed benefit, provides greater protection, provided an example; alternative 2 is a breakwater design with a groin at the south end of project area, showed examples of a breakwater; alternative 3B is recommended with living shoreline and breakwater, 3A is similar but includes a groin; spoke to variations; alternatives to design items such as oyster balls versus toe stone; recommending 3B, cost estimated around $4 million.\par

\par
Mayor Wilkinson questioned what is needed tonight; Dr. Danchuk spoke to getting feedback regarding the recommendation and next step to move forward with design and permitting; to provide a proposal. \par

\par

\par

\par
Deputy Mayor Shelly requested clarification on recommendation; Dr. Danchuk stated alternative 3B was recommendation, however southern protection is needed which will be determined though modeling, so alternative 3A is closer to what will be utilized for modeling; spoke to next step of process.\par
\par
Commissioner Kelly commented on seeing oyster balls in other areas; very effective at stopping erosion and preventing damage; requested clarification on erosion; Dr. Danchuk stated erosion is at 3.5 ft and if not addressed, it will be close to road and impact infrastructure.\par
\par
Deputy Mayor Shelly questioned what more is needed regarding surface water coming down the hill; Dr. Danchuk spoke to best management practices in report; vegetation at top can help slow down as well.\par
\par
Ms. Lancaster stated staff is supportive of conservative recommendation that protects the shoreline and taking into account work that needs done on the slope itself.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs22 Infrastructure Board Members present (in audience): Shon Flaharty, Gayle Grady, George Mariani\par
\par
Mayor Wilkinson stated this is the only item on agenda.\par
\par
Gay Lancaster-Town Manager-provided information regarding why item is being revisited; when plan and design work began on phase III, the Belleair Country Club raised concern on path location; phase I was paused until a determination was made on location; continuing with phase III design, SHPO meetings regarding bridge, will be removed and memorialized; Mr. Hobach and Mr. Shaughnessy presented alternative concept for path location; now at 60% plans and seeking Commission confirmation before moving to 100% plans.\par
\par
Ashley Bernal-Assistant Town Manager-stated from 2024-2026 engineers have indicated that construction costs have gone down; the Finance and Infrastructure Boards met and recommended option A; spoke to project construction of phase I, delay of approximately 8 months of phase III due to SHPO meetings.\par
\par
Mayor Wilkinson stated staff will present then open to public comment.\par
\par
Ms. Bernal presented Option A which is the current phase III design; 8ft shared use path on west, new bridge, 3 way stop at Eastleigh, 6ft sidewalk on east; design estimated completion, construction could begin end of this year, design budget, total $6.01 million total project cost; $2.611 million of funding from state appropriations, with approximately $3.4 million gap to fund.\par
\par
Deputy Mayor Shelly asked if funding included the bridge. Ms. Bernal clarified.\par
\par
Ms. Bernal presented option B resident concept; nothing on west side, 8ft shared use on east; Belleair Country Club offered right of way on west; 3 way stop may be removed, design completion and design delay by a year; design budget to increase by about $500,000, construction cost decrease leaving about $300,000 in total budget; waiting to hear back from Pinellas County, lift station may need moved, not confirmed by county yet; in 2023 points of conflict with driveways and intersections were of concern.\par
\par
Commissioner Kelly questioned expense of moving road. Ms. Bernal stated approximately $300,000 and there could be additional, expense to the Town. \par
\par
Ms. Bernal prepared to present option C, Commission declined. \par
\par
Mayor Wilkinson opened floor to public comment.\par
\par
Mike Pace-N. Pine Circle, former President of Belleair Country Club-thanked for fixing parking. Spoke in support of option B, thinks option A will be underutilized; spoke to golf balls, safety issue, may need to post signage; prepared to give Town land along west side of road.\par
\par
John Hobach- 301 Woodlawn Ave.-spoke to lack of landscape buffer next to sidewalk; making it as safe as possible; spoke in support of Option B, doesn't believe delay is primary issue.\par
\par
Tom Galvin-49 Overbrook Dr.-member of BCC, supporting Option A and opposing Option B; spoke to prior decision, supports that vote; speed reduced along roadway; believes option B is less safe with no conflicts, request the Commission to keep option A.\par
\par
Riley Mortimer-309 Eastleigh-spoke on safety, prefers option A but is ok with either, importance with child safety, wants to move quickly.\par
\par
Brian Battaglia-505 Osceola Rd.-thanked all for their service; spoke to weighing safety concerns as well as costs; supports Option A, most financially feasible.\par
\par
Piers Davies-851 Indian Rocks Rd.-spoke in support previously; still is in support of Option A; commented on potential impacts on east side in regards to vehicle and pedestrian safety; spoke to average daily traffic count of over 13,000 vehicles; additional costs and delays if other option is chosen; urges Commission to stay within option A.\par
\par
Jim Dieringer-614 Palm Ave.-spoke in support of Option B; supports keeping entire path on the same side for safety.\par
\par
Mark Scully-125 Belleview Blvd.-commended for data sharing; spoke to background in real estate development experience; prior experience with roadway use and pathway in Colorado; Belleair is residential and needs to be safe; supports Option B having a wider sidewalk for pedestrians without having to cross road; potential to stamp road for bikes, soft path potential on opposite side to maintain greenspace.\par
\par
Ray Ferrara-3 Seaside Lane.-thanked Commission and staff; is a member of BCC and on the board of directors; club favors path on east side of road (option B); spoke to green and balls, a green fence with likely have to be put up if path is on west side; club prepared to cede some property if moved to east side; \par
\par
Laurie Adams-321 Overbrook Dr.-spoke in support of Option A; commented on safety, vehicles more dangerous than golf balls, west side is best for aesthetics and safety, fulfills ordinance requirements for sidewalks; option for pedestrian crossing signal if 3 way stop is not wanted.\par
\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs22 Ms. Lancaster stated Mr. Carpenter will provide some basic structure to be able to approve millage; spoke to audit and healthy reserve balance, when hurricanes hit reserves were used, have not been reimbursed yet for it all; reserves are healthy but necessary to match state funding for CIP projects; Indian Rocks Road III to begin this year and then phase II which will require reserves. \par
\par
Mr. Carpenter stated budget is a year round process that is monitored; 2026-2027 funds are all balanced as proposed; general fund is a $12.7 million budget; large majority of revenue to general fund is ad valorem property tax, other revenues are from the electric franchise fee, sewer pass through and administration overhead, recreation and police dept bring in for off duty, other sources are interest for investments; majority of increase resides in the Police Department and town-wide operations due to Largo Fire contract and police collective bargaining agreement.\par
\par
Ms. Lancaster spoke to police bargaining negotiation; looked at small departments around the county and competition and were at the bottom, goal was to get in the middle and be competitive.\par
\par
Mr. Carpenter continued presentation by providing overview of all general fund departments; proposed budget includes a 4% average merit increase for all staff, health insurance increased at 2.5% which is well below national average; spoke to no change in Town Manager operating; Town Clerk reduced operating costs; Finance Department changes to staffing and bank service fees; Human Resources reduced costs for personnel lawyer services; Town-wide Services major changes include Pinellas County sewer pass through, Largo Fire agreement, property and casualty insurance for the Town, utilities (power, water, sewer, internet), IT, building and maintenance costs, library co-op reimbursements; Communications Department small increase to operating for ADA compliance; Police Department increases due to bargaining contract, pension contributions; Parks Department increases for Christmas decorations and park amenities; Streets Department had decrease to operating for street sweeping contract, NPDS contract and other stormwater activities moved to stormwater fund; Recreation Department brings in revenue through fees, not fully self-sufficient, increase to field trips and software upgrade; Town Events fairly same year after year; available for questions on general fund; none. \par
\par
Mr. Carpenter discussed the Capital Projects fund, the Town has a conservative policy to maintain a 15% balance for equipment replacement; listed capital projects to be done, approximately $12 million; revenues are Penny for Pinellas, utility service tax, Belleair Country Club land lease on west course; staff efforts to get grants for projects is significant; cost for maintaining buildings is in this account as well, town hall and recreation center have substantial needs, largely roofs on both buildings, restroom in town hall, hardening of Dimmitt Center for security, kitchen in recreation; need to maintain and keep compliant and safe; Capital Project fund also pays debt; discussed debt total.\par
\par
Mr. Carpenter spoke to Special Revenue funds which are all restricted; Local Option Fuel Tax, Transportation Impact Fund, Tree Replacement Fund, and Stormwater Fund; good fund balance in stormwater, can be source of revenue to help with future project costs, would like to think in terms of the future. \par
\par
Mr. Carpenter next addressed the enterprise funds which are funded fully through fees; Water fund, Pinellas County increases by 5% which will be passed along; Solid Waste fund, Pinellas is charging 8% increase in tipping fees, no increase to recycling, requesting a 5% increase to solid waste bill which is approximately $3.04 per month; Building Permit fund has a strong balance, fully funded by permitting and inspection fees.\par
\par
Ms. Lancaster stated this budget doesn't include any additional personnel, will maintain flat; Finance Board stated commitment to millage was to set 25% away annually, initial budget had 20%, but have adjusted to maintain 25%; is a matter of trust and will bring a final budget that contains those changes to maintain 25% in the Capital Projects.\par
\par
Mr. Carptenter next discussed millage; property appraiser provided taxable values; tax calendar lags budget by one year; Belleair has been a leader year over year for appraised and taxable values; millage as proposed is the same as last two years at 6.977 mills, which generates $9.8 million of revenue; requirement that Commission review and adopt proposed millage for TRIM notices to be sent out; announced upcoming budget hearing dates.\par
\par

\par
Mr. Womack next spoke to emergency response; all public works departments come together to respond; spoke to previous storms, since hurricane Irma, we have consistently been one of the first communities fully operational following storm; planning and preparation, long employee hours to remove debris, preventative pumps to be deployed; roadway clearing; spoke to staff response to water breaks on holidays and after hours, lights acquired to be able to provide night response, employees available 24/7 to respond and assess; a reduction of property tax revenue would require a close look at how to provide the service level residents have come to expect.\par
\par
Mr. Womack discussed the projected operating budget for FY 27; personnel, operating expenses; Introduced, Wilfred Holmes-Solid Waste Director, Mike King-Parks and Streets Manager, Chuck Guara-Water Distribution Manager. \par
Mentioned Tena, who has served for 42 years, and Terry Williams has been here 41 years, spoke to experience and institutional knowledge, chart is not just percentages, it's the people. Parks and streets services are 100% funded through general fund, there are currently no additional revenue sources to fund these operations; solid waste and water have different funding sources, but still rely on other departments; showed slide on permitted uses of property tax revenue, still unanswered questions on how funding will work, parks maintenance is not listed; spoke to impacts such as preventative maintenance, response times, athletic field upkeep, emergency response preparedness and capacity; work in one department often supports another, so impacts in one area will affect all; level of service provided is directly connected to resources available to support it. \par
\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs22 Chief Doyle spoke to significant part of policing is being proactive; primary responsibility is public safety and community policing. Spoke to services of personnel involved in fraud and economic crime investigations, house checks, Operation Medicine Cabinet, code enforcement; a well-run department identifies problems early; showed example of code enforcement actions; continued discussing additional services such as scanning pets for microchips, community event support, bike helmet program, special details and dignitary security, special relief permits and related operations, agency partnerships with PCSO, Clearwater, Largo Police Department, Secret Service and FBI, while maintaining local control of policing in Belleair.\par
\par
Chief Doyle spoke to the police department and emergency response; manage emergency operations center, first sweep of debris removal and roadway clearing, assess conditions, respond to emergency, manage detours and closures, use meters to detect live electricity for live wires, spoke to Helene response and no resources, two officers got into a kayak to check on residents; prevented looting during emergency, Belleair was among one of the first communities to reopen after the storms, all departments were involved.\par
\par
Chief Doyle continued presentation by speaking about the financial side, FY 2027 budget; for public safety is $4.46 million, which is 61% of the general funds property tax revenue; of that, the Police Department budget is $3.4 million, majority of that is personnel, listed number of sworn full-time, sworn part-time, non-sworn full-time and sworn reserved with an average of 29 years of law enforcement experience, training dollars saved, benefits through use of part-time officers; operating expenses keeps dept functioning, reducing the budget affects personnel and services, not discretionary spending; 93.4% of the Police Department budget comes from the general fund and revenue for Pelican security. The Police Department depends on the general fund to provide the service residents expect.\par
\par
Chief Doyle spoke to proposed changes regarding permitted use of property tax revenue; public safety is one, but doesn't operate in a vacuum, additional department support is needed, no funding in legislation to support; emphasized Police Department services are not necessarily protected at current level; potential service impacts were addressed, reductions in resources due to need to prioritize immediate calls for service; diminished local control over community priorities, emergency preparedness and hurricane response.\par
\par
Chief Doyle concluded presentation by noting typically 1-3 minutes to respond to 911 calls; difficult to put a dollar value on immediate control and a department that is dedicated specifically to Belleair, if forced to reduce funding, question is what services will need to be given up, reduced or delayed to absorb the loss.\par
\par

\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs22 Gay Lancaster-Town Manager-spoke to prior discussions regarding Amendment 3; 10% of voters have submitted their mail in ballots; speaks to reading full language; for homesteaded properties only, instructs legislature to increase exemption up to all remaining assessed valuation; spoke to an example of a typical tax bill, split roughly by thirds; Belleair tax is unique in that 76% of properties are homesteaded, chart presented which reflects homestead percentage; 71.3% of general fund revenue comes from property tax revenue, other sources are only 28.7% of the budget; spoke to total received and breakdown; provided a chart of how a dollar is broken down; important to show how every dollar is accounted for; spoke next to public safety, $4.46 million goes to it; property tax relief with a taxable value of $500,000 has an exemption currently of $51,411; if amendment passes, in year 1, they will benefit $150,000 of exemption; in year 2, $250,000 worth of exemption; showed a graphic of budget impacts; legislation dictates how remaining tax dollars can be spent, it doesn't include parks, recreation, events, and beautification; state telling how community can spend; doesn't stop at $250,000 exemption, intention is to eliminate all remaining valuation for homesteaded properties; future increases have no voter input, legislature is charged with elimination; if fully eliminated, $3.3 million would be left, which isn't enough to cover public safety costs.\par
\par
Ms. Lancaster stated she doesn't feel people are aware of the full implication of the amendment; for towns like ours it is very significant; stressing that people may not be aware of the fine print; will be making a presentation to the Belleair Country Club at their request; thanked those in audience for attending.\par
\par
Mayor Wilkinson asked if anyone in the audience had questions.\par
\par
Bill Brancaccio- resident-spoke to reduction in first year; questioned impact. Ms. Lancaster said first year would be 11% less, then 21% less in second year; Mr. Brancaccio spoke to prior experience living in Belleair Beach and PCSO service contract, but impacts will be seen all around.\par
\par
Commissioner Kelly spoke to prior comments on state decisions dictating how small communities can spend their tax dollars; need to be cautious of the fine print and state making decisions on how money can be spent.\par
\par
\par
